newsitem.title: UK: Britain suspicious of US-style telemedicine.
newsitem.headline: Britain suspicious of US-style telemedicine.

text.p: British doctors said on Monday they were wary of US-style advances in telemedicine and hoped to proceed more carefully with the technology.

Using monitors linked by telephone line, video links and other advances had helped free up hospital beds, but risked domination by companies bent only on profits, they told a conference on telemedicine.

Richard Wootton, director of the Institute of Telemedicine at Belfast's Queen's University, said he wanted to see telemedicine integrated into Britain's National Health Service as routine. But he said it should be done cautiously.

"Some of the glitz and glamour shouldn't be allowed to eclipse the more practical matters such as whether it is more cost-effective," he said ahead of an international conference at Britain's Royal Society of Medicine.

Delegates were being shown dramatic evidence of how telemedicine can work, including demonstrations of remote-controlled brain surgery and a live link to events surrounding Hong Kong's handover to China.
Wootton said he was worried at how some equipment manufacturers dominated the debate in countries like the United States.
"What we've seen in the States is telemedicine becoming a major commercial act in some spheres," he told a news briefing.

"Some of us are concerned that major commercial interests are amassing in the wings...who will try to drive the development of telemedicine before it can be shown to be a cost-effective method of health care."
This had already started to happen in Britain, he said.

"There are equipment manufacturers who we know are talking to hospital managers and telling them if they buy their particular brand of equipment they will be able to practise telemedicine," Wootton said.
"Buying a box won't allow you to do telemedicine any more than buying a scalpel will allow you to become a surgeon."
Other areas also needed to be examined, said Sir Christopher Paine, president of the Royal Society of Medicine.
"The risks include things like patient confidentiality...and the risk the patient isn't always face-to-face with the doctor," Paine said.
But the rewards of telemedicine could be considerable, several doctors told the conference.
Paul Johnson, a clinical physiologist at Oxford's John Radcliffe Hospital, said telemedicine had helped free up 10 percent of beds for babies and young children in the Oxford area.
Some of the babies had been born prematurely, and their underdeveloped lungs were vulnerable to infection. "A little infection can tip them over," he said.

Yet such babies did much better at home, with their families. Telemedicine allowed a worried parent to hook small monitors to a baby and send data down the telephone to doctors. This would allow doctors to decide if the baby should be brought in.
"There's the potential for closing up to 25 percent of beds," Johnson predicted.
